newsitem.title: USA: Wholesale prices fall 0.3 percent in January.
newsitem.headline: Wholesale prices fall 0.3 percent in January.

text.p: Prices at the wholesale level fell for the first time in over two years in January, the Labour Department said Friday, new evidence that inflationary pressures remained largely contained despite the maturity of the economic expansion.
The department said the Producer Price Index fell 0.3 percent last month after rising a revised 0.6 percent in December.
Excluding the often-volatile food and energy sector, the so-called core rate that economists believe more closely tracks inflation, was unchanged in January after being up 0.1 percent in December.
The decline was unexpected by Wall Street, which had forecast an overall increase of 0.3 percent, with the core rate up 0.2 percent.
"Whoosh! It almost leaves you speechless," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "It doesn't say much for forecasters.
"Despite the fact that the economy has been recovering since March of 1991, there are still are very few signs of upward pressure on prices," he added. "That's very, very unusual."
The January decline was the first since a 0.4 percent drop in October, 1994.

The department said energy prices declined 0.2 percent last month after jumping 3.4 percent in December. Gasoline prices, however, rose 2.6 percent, although this was offset by a 2.8 percent decline in home heating oil.
Food prices also moved lower, by 1.0 percent, as meat and fruit prices declined. Tobacco prices edged up 0.1 percent.
Passenger car prices dropped 0.4 percent after a 0.1 percent increase in December.
Goods at the intermediate level of production, which require additional processing, rose 0.2 percent after gaining 0.3 percent in December.
Prices at the early part of the production cycle, for so-called crude goods, jumped 5.2 percent after being up 4.9 percent in December.
The department previously reported that overall prices rose 0.5 percent in December.
